overview.text: A graphics processing unit (GPU) is a specialized processor that accelerates the creation and processing of images by handling many data elements in parallel. Graphics work often involves repeating similar calculations across many vertices, fragments, or pixels; a GPU’s many computing units can work on those tasks at the same time. This design also makes GPUs useful beyond graphics: when a task can be divided into many similar calculations, a GPU can help speed video work, scientific computing, and machine-learning workloads. A GPU may be integrated alongside a CPU or installed as a discrete chip. A graphics card is a larger add-in board that contains a GPU and other supporting components. GPUs complement CPUs rather than simply replacing them.

key_facts.text: GPUs were originally designed to accelerate graphics rendering, including 3D images.
Parallel processing means working on multiple data elements at once; graphics calculations often suit this approach.
GPUs can accelerate some non-graphics tasks, including machine learning, video editing, and scientific computing.
A GPU may be integrated with a computer’s CPU or provided as a discrete chip.
A graphics card is an add-in board that contains a GPU and other components; the terms “GPU” and “graphics card” do not mean exactly the same thing.
